extracted.intended_audience: mass-communication/media scholars and researchers (journalism studies, online news production, media theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers on applying and adapting Shoemaker and Reese’s hierarchy-of-influences model to newer/digital media contexts (online journalism, individual web content, cross-platform newsrooms). Advises when levels apply, how layers interact, and how the visual model might be made dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual level of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of content is influenced by individual communicators, such as the classic ‘gatekeeper’ (the individual content producer occupying the center core of the model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The individual sits at the core of the concentric model and can influence content idiosyncratically, but is typically constrained by outer layers (routines, organization, extramedia, ideology). Examples: David Manning White’s ‘Mr. Gates’; in newer-media contexts individuals may exert greater influence when routines are absent or thin. Note the warning that researchers should avoid extrapolating from individuals to higher levels without caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media routines level of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Content selection is influenced by communication routines: norms of selection that have evolved over the history of mass communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routines often strongly constrain individual decisions, forming cohesive rules that ensure predictability (e.g., TV news technical/production routines, standard story lengths). In newer media, routines may be absent, unstable, or changing—allowing individuals more influence. Empirical examples include changing cross-platform newsroom practices and online-first newsroom experiments. Researchers should assess whether routines for the medium under study are established before assuming their constraining power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational level of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Group decision-making and organizational structures within specific media settings affect content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational constraints can limit individual autonomy (editorial policies, chain of command). However, the placement of organizational influence above media routines is contested. For lone-web producers or independent bloggers, the organizational level may be irrelevant and can legitimately be omitted from analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia (social institution/market) level of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is influenced by factors outside the medium such as markets, audiences, advertisers, interest groups, and legal constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extramedia forces include marketplace pressures, audience preferences, advertisers, and legal/regulatory constraints (privacy, defamation). In moments of upheaval these constraints can shift—altering their influence on content—and should be explicitly considered in analysis of newer media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological (social system) level of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is influenced by the broader social system or ideology; the most macro level that subsumes other influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoemaker and Reese characterize ideology/social system as the outermost and most powerful level. Researchers should recognize how prevailing ideologies can 'subsum[e] all the others' and, in times of political upheaval, how ideological shifts can change or reorder other levels' influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy/power-differential assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The model implies that some levels of influence are generally more powerful than others (the notion of a hierarchy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concentric-circles visualization suggests differential power (ideology > extramedia > organizational > routines > individual). The paper notes critiques: U.S.-centrism, unclear rationale for ordering (e.g., organizational above routines), and empirical difficulty in separating and comparing effects across levels. Researchers should not accept the ordering uncritically and must address empirical identification of level-specific effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for lack/instability of routines in newer media
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must consider that many newer-media sectors lack consistent, established production routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When routines are unsolidified (e.g., early-stage online journalism, converging cross-platform newsrooms), individuals may exercise greater influence. Use organizational-change concepts (Lewin’s unfreeze/transition/refreeze) to understand the durability of routines. Empirical evidence (survey/studies cited) shows rapid routine change; researchers should empirically assess routine stability rather than assume their presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow levels to be breached, thinned, or eliminated (dynamic-layer model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconceptualize the visual model so layers are dynamic: any layer can 'thin', be 'breached' by forces from below, or disappear when warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than static concentric circles, visualize influence as dynamic layers that can be weakened or bypassed (e.g., weak media routines allow individual producers to 'burst out' of the core). Examples include a copy editor using Twitter because 'no one told her not to' and revolutionary periods where ideology/extramedia shift. The paper recommends adapting the visualization to reflect fluid interplays among levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat individual-produced online content as distinct (omit organizational level when warranted)
rubrics_metrics.description: For content produced by individuals not affiliated with organizations (blogs, Twitter, Facebook), the organizational level may be irrelevant and can be omitted from analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual online producers remain subject to ideological and extramedia constraints and to emergent conventions (some routines), but organizational constraints may not apply. Shoemaker and Reese acknowledge that 'any given study cannot address all these levels at once,' so scholars are justified in excluding levels that do not pertain to their phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Span multiple levels of analysis where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should attempt to examine connections among multiple levels of influence rather than focusing on a single level in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoemaker and Vos urged more studies to span multiple levels; the paper echoes this while noting methodological difficulties in empirically separating level effects. Researchers should design studies to capture interlevel interplay when feasible, but also be explicit about which levels are being addressed and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be attentive to cross-platform, national, regional, and contextual differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches to creating and overseeing online news differ across national boundaries, within nations, and across regions; cross-platform convergence complicates routine formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work shows no single industry standard for dual print/online publishing and rapid, uneven changes in newsroom routines. Researchers must avoid overgeneralizing from one context and should account for platform-specific and locale-specific institutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theory flexibly to adapt to a changing media environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars should critically reexamine and adapt existing media theories and conceptual frameworks for the digital era rather than abandon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Echoing Morris and Ogan, the paper calls for creative application and methodological adaptation of theory to changing media configurations (multimedia professional journalism and individual digital content). The reconceptualized, dynamic hierarchy is framed as a way to preserve the usefulness of Shoemaker and Reese’s model while making it fit 21st-century realities.
